arml-1995-individual-01.title: Geometric series
arml-1995-individual-01.body:
Expanding the nest gives $3^{11}+3^{10}+\dots+3+1=\dfrac{3^{12}-1}{3-1}$. Now $3^{12}-1=(3^6-1)(3^6+1)=728\cdot730=(2^3\cdot7\cdot13)(2\cdot5\cdot73)$. Dividing by $2$, the number is $2^3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot13\cdot73$ and its largest prime factor is $73$.

**Answer: 73**

arml-1995-individual-02.title: Triangle inequality
arml-1995-individual-02.body:
The ratio of areas is $\left(\frac{AC}{MP}\right)^2=\left(\frac{AC}8\right)^2$. We need $AC<BC=60$ and, by the triangle inequality, $AC>60-12=48$. So $36<\frac{AC^2}{64}<56.25$, and the integer values are $37,38,\dots,56$ (twenty values). Their sum is $\frac{(37+56)\cdot20}2=930$.

**Answer: 930**

arml-1995-individual-03.title: Factor
arml-1995-individual-03.body:
$p^{1994}+p^{1995}=p^{1994}(1+p)$ and $p^{1994}$ is a perfect square, so $1+p$ must be a perfect square: $1+p=t^2$, $p=(t-1)(t+1)$. A prime has the factorisation $1\cdot p$, so $t-1=1$, $t=2$, $p=3$. Check: $3^{1994}\cdot4=(2\cdot3^{997})^2$.

**Answer: 3**

arml-1995-individual-04.title: The quotient is always 2
arml-1995-individual-04.body:

In the six numerators each of $A,B,C$ appears twice in each of the hundreds, tens and units places, so the numerator is $\frac{222(A+B+C)}{999}=\frac{2(A+B+C)}{9}$. The denominator is $\frac{A+B+C}{9}$. So $k=2$ whenever $A+B+C\ne0$, and $k$ is undefined for $(0,0,0)$. Hence all $10^3-1=999$ triples work.

**Answer: 999**

arml-1995-individual-05.title: Classify planes

arml-1995-individual-06.title: Sophie Germain style
arml-1995-individual-06.body:
Write $x^4+k=(x^2+n)^2-2nx^2$ with $n^2=k$ (so $k$ must be a perfect square), which factors as $(x^2-\sqrt{2n}\,x+n)(x^2+\sqrt{2n}\,x+n)$. The factors have integer coefficients iff $\sqrt{2n}$ is an integer, i.e. $2n=s^2$ with $s$ even, $n=2t^2$, $k=n^2=4t^4$.

$k=4t^4\le2000$ gives $t^4\le500$, so $t=1,2,3,4$: $k=4,64,324,1024$ ($t=5$ gives $2500>2000$).

**Answer: $4,64,324,1024$**

arml-1995-individual-07.title: Intersect on the line y = x
arml-1995-individual-07.body:
$f$ is increasing, so $f$ and $f^{-1}$ (reflections of each other in $y=x$, both increasing) can only meet on $y=x$. Thus we count solutions of $f(x)=x$, i.e. $\sqrt{x+2}=x-c$, which is equivalent to $x\ge c$ and $x+2=(x-c)^2$, i.e. $x^2-(2c+1)x+c^2-2=0$.

Two distinct real roots need discriminant $(2c+1)^2-4(c^2-2)=4c+9>0$, i.e. $c>-\frac94$. Both roots must also satisfy $x\ge c$ (and then $x\ge-2$ automatically). The smaller root is $\frac{2c+1-\sqrt{4c+9}}2$ and it is $\ge c$ iff $1-\sqrt{4c+9}\ge0$, i.e. $\sqrt{4c+9}\le1$, $c\le-2$. At $c=-2$ the roots are $-2$ and $-1$ and both work. So exactly two intersection points occur for $-\frac94<c\le-2$.

**Answer: $-2.25<c\le-2$**

arml-1995-individual-08.title: Factor the trigonometric equation
arml-1995-individual-08.body:
$\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y=\cos x\cos y+\sin x\sin y$ rearranges to $(\sin x-\cos x)(\cos y-\sin y)=0$, so $x=\frac\pi4+n\pi$ or $y=\frac\pi4+n\pi$ for an integer $n$: the solutions are the points of the circle of radius $R=\frac{1995\pi}4$ lying on the vertical lines $x=\frac\pi4+n\pi$ or the horizontal lines $y=\frac\pi4+n\pi$.

*Vertical lines.* For $x>0$: $x=\frac{(4n+1)\pi}4<R$ iff $4n+1\le1993$, $n=0,\dots,498$: $499$ lines, each meeting the circle twice: $998$ points. For $x<0$: $x=-\frac{(4m-1)\pi}4$, $m=1,\dots,499$, $499$ lines of which the last ($4m-1=1995$) is tangent: $498\cdot2+1=997$ points. Total $1995$.

*Horizontal lines* give $1995$ points likewise. No point lies on both a vertical and a horizontal line, since $(4a+1)^2+(4b+1)^2\equiv2\pmod 8$ while $1995^2$ is odd. Hence the total is $2\cdot1995=3990$.

**Answer: 3990**

arml-1995-individual-tb1.title: Ellipse
arml-1995-individual-tb1.body:
If $Q$ has radius $r$, then $MQ=10-r$ and $PQ=r+2$, so $MQ+PQ=12$: $Q$ lies on an ellipse with foci $M(0,0)$, $P(8,0)$ and major axis $12$. Its centre is $(4,0)$, $a=6$, $c=4$, $b^2=36-16=20$. The maximum $y$ is $b=\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt5$.

**Answer: $2\sqrt5$**

arml-1995-individual-tb2.title: Coordinates
arml-1995-individual-tb2.body:
Put the centre of the circle at the origin; the square has half-side $\frac{\sqrt2}2$. The top segment has height $1-\frac{\sqrt2}2$, so circle $P$ has radius $r=\frac{2-\sqrt2}4$ and centre $P=(0,\frac{\sqrt2}2+r)$. By symmetry $Q=(-\frac{\sqrt2}2-r,0)$. The line $PQ$ has slope $1$: $y=x+\frac{\sqrt2}2+r$.

It meets the top side $y=\frac{\sqrt2}2$ at $A=(-r,\frac{\sqrt2}2)$ and the left side $x=-\frac{\sqrt2}2$ at $B=(-\frac{\sqrt2}2,r)$. So $AB=\sqrt2\left(\frac{\sqrt2}2-r\right)=\sqrt2\cdot\frac{3\sqrt2-2}{4}=\frac{3-\sqrt2}2$.

**Answer: $\frac{3-\sqrt2}2$**
